description: Multi-dimensional adversarial review of a diff or capability: correctness, security, and spec compliance, with every finding adversarially verified before it is reported.

findings.title: Format-tip fallback can return an example that is CORRECT (it reveals an answer) or UNPARSEABLE
findings.evidence: `return candidates.firstOrNull { Grader.grade(spec, RawInput.Text(it))?.correct == false } ?: candidates.last()` falls back to the last candidate without grading it. If no candidate grades WRONG, that last candidate is either CORRECT or unreadable. This can happen with a wide tolerance, for example INTEGER accepted `0` with tolerance `1000000`, which makes every example from `-271828` to `9999` CORRECT. The tip would then show an accepted answer to the child. That breaks spec rule 3 ('checking <example> against the part gives WRONG … never reveals an accepted answer'). The property test only uses tolerance `1`, so it never reaches the fallback.
findings.suggestion: Never return an example that has not been graded. When every candidate is CORRECT, build one that is guaranteed to be outside the tolerance (for example max(accepted) + tolerance + 1, written in the part's notation and unit and checked as WRONG). If even that fails, use a tip template with no example. Add a golden or property case with a large tolerance.

findings.title: A negative `exactDecimals` makes the checker throw, despite its documented 'never throws for any spec' guarantee
findings.evidence: `whole + "," + FRACTION_DIGITS.take(exactDecimals)`: Kotlin's `String.take(n)` throws IllegalArgumentException when n < 0. So a DECIMAL spec with `exactDecimals = -1` and any unreadable input throws from `AnswerChecker.check`. design.md and the AnswerChecker KDoc both promise it never throws for any input or spec. The contract caps the value at 0..6, but `AnswerSpec` in the domain does not enforce that. For values above 6, `take` silently gives only 6 digits, so the tip example has the wrong number of decimals: it grades WRONG for its format and misleads the child.
findings.suggestion: Either validate `exactDecimals in 0..6` when the domain `AnswerSpec` is built (an `init { require(...) }` that the slice 5/7 adapters map to a 400), or clamp/coerce in `decimalExamples` so the example always has exactly `exactDecimals` digits. Add a property case that uses random `exactDecimals`.

findings.title: Unit value matching ignores which accepted entry the unit belongs to; correctness depends on an authoring invariant the checker never checks
findings.evidence: `val partUnit = accepted.firstOrNull()?.unit` takes the part's unit from the first accepted value only. Then `accepted.any { Rational.within(input.number.value, it.number.value, tolerance) }` compares the number against every accepted value without checking that value's unit. With accepted `["5 m", "500 cm"]`, the input `500 m` is CORRECT and `500 cm` is WRONG. The contract says all accepted values share one unit (400 at authoring), but authoring validation is out of scope until slice 5, and design.md says 'the checker trusts its spec'.
findings.suggestion: Compare the input only against accepted entries whose unit key equals the input's (or the part's) unit. Alternatively, have the checker treat accepted values with a different unit as unreadable, so they never match, and document the invariant at the domain boundary.

findings.title: The catalog loads lazily inside the first UNPARSEABLE check, so a missing key surfaces at runtime as an initializer error and not at startup
findings.evidence: `private val TIPS ... ResourceBundle.getBundle("messages", ...).let { bundle -> AnswerType.entries.associateWith { bundle.getString(...) } }` runs in the static initializer of `FormatTips`, and the first `tipFor` call triggers it. If a key is missing, that first check throws ExceptionInInitializerError and every later check throws NoClassDefFoundError: a raw 500 on the child submission path, not the fail-fast at boot that design.md describes. It also means the first check of a running JVM does classpath file I/O, which works against the spec's 'no … file access while checking'.
findings.suggestion: Load the tips eagerly when the application starts, for example by touching `FormatTips` from a startup hook in the module that wires the checker in slice 7. Alternatively, expose an `AnswerChecker.selfCheck()` that a Spring context test and startup call, so a broken catalog fails the boot rather than the first child answer.

findings.title: The space-character set is defined twice, as a regex class and as a hand-coded predicate
findings.evidence: `private fun isSpace(c: Char): Boolean = c.code == 0x20 || c.code == 0xA0 || c.code == 0x2009` duplicates `NumericNotation.SPACE_CLASS = "[   ]"`, which the same file already uses for `MIXED`. If the allowed separators change (for example adding U+202F narrow no-break space), the grouping rule and the around-the-slash rule will drift apart without anyone noticing.
findings.suggestion: Define the separator set once in NumericNotation (for example a `SPACE_CHARS` string plus a predicate derived from it), and build both the regex class and the slash trimming from it.

findings.title: The format-tip example works as an answer-key oracle: skipped examples show the child which values are correct, and the fallback example can be a correct answer (FR-27)
findings.evidence: example() goes through a fixed, public list of candidates (INTEGER: 12, 305, 48, -7, …; DECIMAL: 5,2, 3,75, …) and uses the first one the same part grades WRONG. If every candidate is CORRECT (for example a broad tolerance), it falls back to candidates.last(), which is an accepted answer. A child can type something unreadable like 'x', which is free because UNPARSEABLE never uses up an attempt (FR-22). Usually the tip says 'třeba 12'. When it says 'třeba 305' instead, 12 is the correct answer. For a NUMBER_WITH_UNIT part the tip also shows the expected unit (taken from accepted[0]). The checker is pure, but AnswerChecker.check returns this formatTip in the PartResult. The planned slice 7 child submission endpoint will pass it to the unauthenticated child as it is. The store spec requirement 'first candidate that the same part grades WRONG' prescribes this behavior, so the docs store needs fixing too.
findings.suggestion: Make the tip example independent of the answer key. Use one fixed example per type, or pick it from a source that doesn't depend on the spec (for DECIMAL, the exactDecimals format is fine). Never return a candidate that grades CORRECT; if none qualifies, leave the example out of the tip. Change the store spec ('Format tips from the message catalog') first, then add golden or property tests showing that the tip text is the same for every accepted value of a given type and format.

findings.title: Checklist results for the rest of this slice: no endpoints, so authz, auth/session, upload, exposure and CORS are not applicable; no issues in injection, secrets, privacy or dependencies
findings.evidence: The diff (slice2-admin-access..HEAD, commit 0120326) adds only the pure cz.doucko.checking module: an AnswerChecker facade, domain parsers and messages.properties tips. findings.title: Format-tip example falls back to a CORRECT (answer-revealing) or non-WRONG candidate when no candidate grades WRONG
findings.evidence: Store spec, Format tip rule 3: 'When `<example>` … is checked against the same part, the verdict is `WRONG`. So the example … never reveals an accepted answer.' Code: `return candidates.firstOrNull { Grader.grade(spec, RawInput.Text(it))?.correct == false } ?: candidates.last()`. The contract allows any tolerance ≥ 0 with no upper bound (openapi.yaml:1608). So INTEGER accepted ['12'] with tolerance '1000000' makes all six candidates (12, 305, 48, -7, 9999, -271828) CORRECT, and the tip shows '-271828', which is an accepted value. The property test only uses tolerance '1' around accepted values from -20 to 20, so this path is never tested.
findings.suggestion: Build a guaranteed-WRONG example instead of falling back. For example, take an accepted value plus (tolerance + 1), formatted in the part's notation and exactDecimals; for DECIMAL with exactDecimals you can also violate the form. Add a property or golden case with a huge tolerance. If some spec makes rule 3 impossible, amend the store spec to say what happens in that case.

findings.title: Golden-table scenario clause 'every scenario input is present with its verdict' is not mechanically checked
findings.evidence: Store scenario 'Golden table size and coverage': '…AND every input named in a scenario of those requirements is present with that scenario's verdict'. GoldenTableTest only asserts the size (≥150), unique ids, at least 5 cases per requirement, and the one NBSP regression case. Nothing compares the table against the spec's scenario inputs. I checked by hand that today all scenario inputs are present (including NBSP, thin space, U+2212, U+2013, U+2014 and the decomposed caron), so the data complies. But if a case is deleted or edited, the build stays green as long as the counts still hold.
findings.suggestion: Add a test that keeps a pinned list of (requirement, type, spec, input, verdict) tuples taken from the store spec scenarios and asserts each one is in golden-table.jsonl. Or tag cases with `scenario:` ids and check that every scenario id appears.

findings.title: Format tips read a classpath file during the first check, and the purity test cannot detect file/process access
findings.evidence: Store spec: 'The checker SHALL make no network, database, file or AI calls while checking (NFR-5).' FormatTips.TIPS is initialized when the object is first used, i.e. inside the first AnswerChecker.check that returns UNPARSEABLE, so `ResourceBundle.getBundle("messages", …)` reads messages.properties during a check. CheckingPurityTest allows all of `java.lang..` and `java.util..`, which includes ClassLoader resource loading, ResourceBundle, ProcessBuilder and Runtime. So the 'no file calls' rule is not actually enforced.
findings.suggestion: Load the catalog eagerly at module start (or accept the one-off load and record it as a spec decision in the delta). Tighten CheckingPurityTest with explicit denies, e.g. no dependency on java.lang.ProcessBuilder/Runtime, java.io, java.nio, java.net, or ResourceBundle outside FormatTips.

findings.title: NUMBER_WITH_UNIT tip can exceed 120 characters for long unit spellings
findings.evidence: Rule 1: 'It is Czech and at most 120 characters long.' The template 'Tohle neumím přečíst. Napiš číslo a jednotku bez mezer v ní, třeba {0}.' is about 70 characters before the example. The example appends `unit.display`, which comes from the accepted values, and neither the checker nor the visible contract limits their length. A unit display longer than about 40 characters makes the tip break rule 1. No golden or property case uses a long unit.
findings.suggestion: Cap the example (drop the unit or fall back to a shorter template when the result would exceed 120), or have authoring validation bound the unit length and cite that limit in the spec. Add a test case for it.

result.reasoning: The finding holds. At FormatTips.kt:55, `candidates.firstOrNull { Grader.grade(...)?.correct == false } ?: candidates.last()` falls back to `candidates.last()` without grading it. Nothing upstream prevents that path. In Grader.kt:38-41 the tolerance is any parsed non-negative rational with no upper bound, so INTEGER accepted=["0"] with tolerance "1000000" makes all six INTEGER examples (12…-271828) CORRECT. The fallback then puts -271828, an accepted answer, into the tip. That is the reveal the KDoc on lines 12-13 says must never happen. Wide tolerance is not the only way in: an accepted list that includes every candidate also triggers it. Severity stays minor because only admins author specs and such a spec is unusual, but the mechanism is real and nothing guards against it.

The bug is real, but it is hard to reach.

**What the code does.** `FormatTips.kt:55` returns `candidates.last()` without grading it when no candidate grades WRONG.

**Nothing upstream stops it.**
- `AnswerSpec.tolerance` (`CheckingModel.kt:17`) is a free `String?`.
- `Grader` only converts it to a `Rational`.
- `Rational.within` checks `|value - target| <= tolerance` with no upper bound.
- There is no check of tolerance size anywhere in `src/main`.

**The example in the finding works.** Take an INTEGER part with accepted `0` and tolerance `1000000`. All six candidates (`12`, `305`, `48`, `-7`, `9999`, `-271828`) are within 1,000,000 of 0, so they all grade CORRECT. The fallback then puts `-271828`, an accepted answer, into the tip. That breaks the documented rule that the tip "never reveals an accepted answer" (class KDoc, spec rule 3). The same thing happens for NUMBER_WITH_UNIT and DECIMAL with a wide tolerance.

**Who can trigger it.** A child cannot make this happen on purpose. The tip only appears after an UNPARSEABLE input, and the spec comes from the admin-authored answer key. So it is not exploitable by an attacker. It is a data-dependent leak: a careless or unusual admin spec (a very large tolerance, or a small accepted set that covers every candidate) would show an accepted value to the child.

**Severity.** It stays at minor. No test covers it, because the property test only uses tolerance 1. The suggested fix is sound: never return an ungraded example, and fall back to a tip with no example if needed.

The finding holds. FormatTips.kt:63 calls `FRACTION_DIGITS.take(exactDecimals)` whenever `exactDecimals` is not null and not 0. Kotlin's `String.take` throws IllegalArgumentException for a negative n. The domain `AnswerSpec` (CheckingModel.kt:14-24) is a plain data class with `exactDecimals: Int? = null`. It has no init/require guard, and nothing in the checking module checks the value; a grep for `require(` finds only the one in Rational. The call path is real: `AnswerChecker.check` calls `Grader.grade`. If that returns null (UNPARSEABLE), it calls `FormatTips.tipFor(spec)`, then `example`, then `decimalExamples(spec.exactDecimals)`. So a DECIMAL spec with exactDecimals = -1 and unreadable input throws. That breaks design.md:61 ("never throws for any input or spec"). The KDoc itself only says "any input". The >6 point also holds: `take(7)` returns all 6 digits. Grader.kt:52 then marks every candidate WRONG because the decimal count doesn't match, so the first candidate is chosen. The tip example then has the wrong number of decimals and misleads the child. Mitigation: the contract caps the value at 0..6, and no adapter builds AnswerSpec from user data yet in this slice. So today this is only reachable through bad admin content or a future adapter that skips validation. That fits the minor severity.

The mechanism is real, but no real user or attacker can trigger it. In `FormatTips.kt:63`, `FRACTION_DIGITS.take(exactDecimals)` would throw IllegalArgumentException for a negative value. For values above 6 it would quietly give a shorter example. `AnswerSpec` (CheckingModel.kt:14) is a plain data class with no `init` validation.

The path is not reachable today:
1. Nothing in `src/main` builds an `AnswerSpec` or calls `AnswerChecker.check`. The only production use of `FormatTips.tipFor` is inside `AnswerChecker` itself, and `checking` is a pure library with no web or persistence adapter yet. No HTTP endpoint, stored content or user input can reach it. Only tests can build a spec with `exactDecimals = -1`.
2. A spec will only come from outside once the slice 5/7 adapters exist. Those adapters will receive admin-authored content through the contract, and the finding itself admits the contract caps `exactDecimals` at 0..6. The generated OpenAPI models and validation reject values outside that range before any domain object is built.
3. Even then, only the authenticated admin writes answer specs, and the child never does. A child's input can only cause the throw if the spec is already invalid, which the contract prevents.

So this is a hardening gap: the KDoc's 'never throws' promise does not hold for specs the contract already forbids. An `init { require(exactDecimals in 0..6) }` would be cheap defence in depth. But it is not an exploitable or reproducible defect for any real user, so I am refuting it under the exploitability lens. If it is kept at all, it should be treated as a hardening nit.

I could not refute it: the code works exactly as the finding describes. In `Grader.numberWithUnit` (`Grader.kt:78-88`), line 80 takes the part's unit from the first parsed accepted entry only. Line 86 checks the input's unit against that one unit. Line 88 then compares the input's number against every accepted entry's number and ignores each entry's own unit. So with accepted `["5 m", "500 cm"]`, the input `500 m` passes the unit check and matches 500 numerically, giving CORRECT. The input `500 cm` fails the unit check, giving WRONG. Why it stays minor and low-confidence: a spec only breaks the checker if it violates the contract invariant, which authoring is supposed to reject with a 400. No production path creates such specs in this slice, so this is defensive hardening, not a live bug. The current minor severity fits.

But nobody can actually trigger the problem. In src/main, nothing outside the checking module builds an AnswerSpec or calls AnswerChecker; only tests and FormatTips use it. The JVM behaviour the finding describes is real, but the defect isn't reachable as claimed, and it misreads the design.

What is accurate: `FormatTips` is a Kotlin `object`. `TIPS` is set in its static initializer, which runs on first use. A `getString` that throws `MissingResourceException` there would surface as `ExceptionInInitializerError`, and every later use would throw `NoClassDefFoundError`.

Why it doesn't hold up:
1. **It misquotes the design.** design.md:67-69 does not promise a fail-fast at boot. It says `FormatTips` "reads every key once when the class loads and fails fast, and the golden table exercises every tip key." The code does exactly that. The design puts the mitigation at build/test time, not at application startup.
2. **A missing key can't reach a running JVM.** `messages.properties` ships in the same jar as the class (src/main/resources, lines 25-31). It has a key for all seven `AnswerType` entries. Because `associateWith` iterates over every `AnswerType.entries`, any test that touches `FormatTips` loads all keys at once. The golden table, property and timing tests hit UNPARSEABLE paths through `AnswerChecker.check`. So a missing or renamed key, or a new enum value, fails `mvn verify` before any artifact exists. Runtime classpath drift isn't plausible for a resource bundled in the same jar.
3. **There's no child submission path yet.** Nothing in src/main calls `AnswerChecker`; the finding itself says the wiring comes in slice 7. The "raw 500 on the child submission path" has no caller in this code.
4. **The "file access while checking" point is weak.** It's a one-time classpath read during class initialization, not per-check I/O. The same kind of lazy init applies to every Kotlin object and regex in the module.

At most this is a hardening suggestion for slice 7 (warm the checker at startup). It is not a correctness defect in this code.

The lazy loading is real: `FormatTips` is a Kotlin `object`, so `TIPS` loads on its first use, from `AnswerChecker.kt:16`. If a key were missing, the first check would throw ExceptionInInitializerError and later checks would throw NoClassDefFoundError. But no real user or attacker can trigger this.

1. A missing key cannot reach a shipped build. The initializer reads the key for every `AnswerType.entries` value at once, not only the one being checked. The golden table has many UNPARSEABLE cases (VN-07, NN-04…, II-*, DI-*, FI-*), so loading the class with any one missing key fails `mvnw verify`. The design.md mitigation ("reads every key once when the class loads and fails fast, and the golden table exercises every tip key") says the same thing, and the build-time gate enforces it. For the bug to appear, someone would have to change the `messages.properties` inside the packaged jar after the build. That is a deploy-tampering scenario, not something a user can cause with input.
2. No child endpoint calls the checker yet. Wiring it into the web layer is slice 7, so no 500 is reachable on any request path today.
3. A child's input cannot change which keys exist. Every input, hostile or not, triggers the same one-time load of a catalog that the tests have already proved complete.
4. The "file access while checking" point applies only once per JVM: one classpath resource read on first use. That is a minor style concern, not a correctness bug.

The startup self-check is a reasonable hardening idea for slice 7, but the claimed failure cannot be reproduced against this build.

I could not refute this finding. The code works the way the finding says, and the problem is real.

**How the example is picked.** `FormatTips.example()` (FormatTips.kt:39-56) goes through a fixed list of candidates and picks the first one that `Grader.grade(spec, …)` marks wrong (`correct == false`). If none is wrong, it falls back to `candidates.last()`. So the example shown depends on the answer key:

Then `accepted.any { Rational.within(input.number.value, it.number.value, tolerance) }` compares the number against every accepted value without checking that value's unit. With accepted `["5 m", "500 cm"]`, the input `500 m` is CORRECT and `500 cm` is WRONG. The contract says all accepted values share one unit (400 at authoring), but authoring validation is out of scope until slice 5, and design.md says 'the checker trusts its spec'.
contested.suggestion: Compare the input only against accepted entries whose unit key equals the input's (or the part's) unit. Alternatively, have the checker treat accepted values with a different unit as unreadable, so they never match, and document the invariant at the domain boundary.
verifierNotes:
I could not refute it: the code works exactly as the finding describes. In `Grader.numberWithUnit` (`Grader.kt:78-88`), line 80 takes the part's unit from the first parsed accepted entry only. Line 86 checks the input's unit against that one unit. Line 88 then compares the input's number against every accepted entry's number and ignores each entry's own unit. So with accepted `["5 m", "500 cm"]`, the input `500 m` passes the unit check and matches 500 numerically, giving CORRECT. The input `500 cm` fails the unit check, giving WRONG. Nothing else in the `checking` module catches this. `AnswerSpec` (`CheckingModel.kt`) has no init/require validation, and its KDoc only says the unit "is derived from `accepted`". The checker therefore relies entirely on the authoring rule that all accepted values share one unit, which is not enforced anywhere in this repo yet.

There is also a related inconsistency in the same area. `FormatTips.kt:47` uses `firstNotNullOfOrNull` to pick the first entry that has a unit. `Grader` uses `accepted.firstOrNull()?.unit`. With accepted `["5", "5 m"]`, the format tips would show "m", but the grader's part unit would be null, so any input written with a unit would be graded WRONG.

Why it stays minor and low-confidence: a spec only breaks the checker if it violates the contract invariant, which authoring is supposed to reject with a 400. No production path creates such specs in this slice, so this is defensive hardening, not a live bug. The current minor severity fits.

rejected.title: The catalog loads lazily inside the first UNPARSEABLE check, so a missing key surfaces at runtime as an initializer error and not at startup
rejected.evidence: `private val TIPS ... ResourceBundle.getBundle("messages", ...).let { bundle -> AnswerType.entries.associateWith { bundle.getString(...) } }` runs in the static initializer of `FormatTips`, and the first `tipFor` call triggers it. If a key is missing, that first check throws ExceptionInInitializerError and every later check throws NoClassDefFoundError: a raw 500 on the child submission path, not the fail-fast at boot that design.md describes. It also means the first check of a running JVM does classpath file I/O, which works against the spec's 'no … file access while checking'.
rejected.suggestion: Load the tips eagerly when the application starts, for example by touching `FormatTips` from a startup hook in the module that wires the checker in slice 7. Alternatively, expose an `AnswerChecker.selfCheck()` that a Spring context test and startup call, so a broken catalog fails the boot rather than the first child answer.
verifierNotes:
The JVM behaviour the finding describes is real, but the defect isn't reachable as claimed, and it misreads the design.

What is accurate: `FormatTips` is a Kotlin `object`. `TIPS` is set in its static initializer, which runs on first use. A `getString` that throws `MissingResourceException` there would surface as `ExceptionInInitializerError`, and every later use would throw `NoClassDefFoundError`.

Why it doesn't hold up:
1. **It misquotes the design.** design.md:67-69 does not promise a fail-fast at boot. It says `FormatTips` "reads every key once when the class loads and fails fast, and the golden table exercises every tip key." The code does exactly that. The design puts the mitigation at build/test time, not at application startup.
2. **A missing key can't reach a running JVM.** `messages.properties` ships in the same jar as the class (src/main/resources, lines 25-31). It has a key for all seven `AnswerType` entries. Because `associateWith` iterates over every `AnswerType.entries`, any test that touches `FormatTips` loads all keys at once. The golden table, property and timing tests hit UNPARSEABLE paths through `AnswerChecker.check`. So a missing or renamed key, or a new enum value, fails `mvn verify` before any artifact exists. Runtime classpath drift isn't plausible for a resource bundled in the same jar.
3. **There's no child submission path yet.** Nothing in src/main calls `AnswerChecker`; the finding itself says the wiring comes in slice 7. The "raw 500 on the child submission path" has no caller in this code.
4. **The "file access while checking" point is weak.** It's a one-time classpath read during class initialization, not per-check I/O. The same kind of lazy init applies to every Kotlin object and regex in the module.

At most this is a hardening suggestion for slice 7 (warm the checker at startup). It is not a correctness defect in this code.

The lazy loading is real: `FormatTips` is a Kotlin `object`, so `TIPS` loads on its first use, from `AnswerChecker.kt:16`. If a key were missing, the first check would throw ExceptionInInitializerError and later checks would throw NoClassDefFoundError. But no real user or attacker can trigger this.

1. A missing key cannot reach a shipped build. The initializer reads the key for every `AnswerType.entries` value at once, not only the one being checked. The golden table has many UNPARSEABLE cases (VN-07, NN-04…, II-*, DI-*, FI-*), so loading the class with any one missing key fails `mvnw verify`. The design.md mitigation ("reads every key once when the class loads and fails fast, and the golden table exercises every tip key") says the same thing, and the build-time gate enforces it. For the bug to appear, someone would have to change the `messages.properties` inside the packaged jar after the build. That is a deploy-tampering scenario, not something a user can cause with input.
2. No child endpoint calls the checker yet. Wiring it into the web layer is slice 7, so no 500 is reachable on any request path today.
3. A child's input cannot change which keys exist. Every input, hostile or not, triggers the same one-time load of a catalog that the tests have already proved complete.
4. The "file access while checking" point applies only once per JVM: one classpath resource read on first use. That is a minor style concern, not a correctness bug.

The startup self-check is a reasonable hardening idea for slice 7, but the claimed failure cannot be reproduced against this build.
